rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The subject of these verses is every stubborn tyrant mentioned in verse 15.
rows.anchor: every stubborn tyrant mentioned in v. 15

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Beyond him lies Hell means that after death the tyrant will go to Hell.
rows.anchor: after his death he will go to Hell

rows.speaker: Q, Z
rows.claim: An alternate reading is that Hell lies before him in this life, as if he stands at its edge about to fall in.
rows.anchor: it can also be read “before him lies Hell,” referring to his state in this world

rows.speaker: Bg, Ṭ
rows.claim: The oozing pus is a mixture of blood and pus.
rows.anchor: a mixture of blood and pus

rows.speaker: Bg, Z
rows.claim: The pus oozes from the bodies of Hell's people.
rows.anchor: which oozes from the bodies of the people in Hell

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: He gulps the liquid because it is bitter and hot.
rows.anchor: because of the liquid’s bitterness and heat

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: He can scarcely swallow because he chokes on the liquid.
rows.anchor: since he will choke on it

rows.speaker: R, Bḍ
rows.claim: Torment affects every part with pains that cause death, but does not kill him; death would otherwise release him from torment.
rows.anchor: each part of his body will be affected by the pains and afflictions that bring about death

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: As ashes vanish in a storm, disbelievers' deeds are nullified because of their disbelief, leaving no trace.
rows.anchor: Like ashes blown about by a stormy wind until no trace of them remains

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One interpretation is that the deeds are good actions, such as charity and feeding the hungry.
rows.anchor: good actions, such as giving charity and feeding the hungry

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that the deeds are evil actions, such as idol worship.
rows.anchor: evil actions, such as worshipping idols

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: A third interpretation is that the deeds combine good and bad actions.
rows.anchor: a combination of both good and bad deeds

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: On Judgment Day, disbelievers receive no trace of heavenly reward for what they did.
rows.anchor: on the Day of Judgment, the disbelievers will not receive even a trace of heavenly reward for their actions

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: This means they will not benefit even from their good deeds.
rows.anchor: the disbelievers will not benefit even from their good actions

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Extreme error means the farthest distance from the path of Truth.
rows.anchor: the farthest distance from the path of Truth

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Extreme error can also mean the profound grief and regret at realizing one's deeds were wasted.
rows.anchor: the extreme grief and regret that the disbelievers will experience upon realizing that their deeds have gone to waste

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran elsewhere describes the deeds of disbelievers as brought to naught.
rows.anchor: For the deeds of the disbelievers being brought to naught, see also, for example, 2:217; 7:147; 18:105.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is late Makkan and likely dates shortly before the migration to Madinah.
rows.anchor: A late Makkan sūrah, al-Naḥl was likely revealed shortly before the migration to Madinah

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some date verses 126–127 to Madinah after Uḥud and see them as guidance for the Prophet responding to the killing and mutilation of Ḥamzah.
rows.anchor: instruct the Prophet about how to respond to the killing and mutilation of his beloved uncle, Ḥamzah (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some consider verse 110 Madinan and about emigrants who left Makkah for Madinah after oppression.
rows.anchor: to refer to those who emigrated from Makkah to Madinah (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Verse 41 is usually understood as referring to Muslims who emigrated from Makkah to Abyssinia before the migration to Madinah.
rows.anchor: usually understood to refer to those Muslims who emigrated from Makkah to Abyssinia several years before the migration of Makkan Muslims to Madinah (Q)

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: An alternative view considers verse 41 Madinan.
rows.anchor: some consider v. 41 to be Madinan as well (IJ)

rows.speaker: Āl, IJ
rows.claim: Other authorities also classify verses 95–97 and 112 as Madinan.
rows.anchor: Others also consider vv. 95–97 (Āl, IJ) and v. 112 (IJ) to be Madinan verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah takes its name from its account of God's revelation to the bee.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from the discussion of God’s revelation to the bee in vv. 68–69.

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Some call it al-Niʿam, The Blessings, because it repeatedly names God's gifts, which verse 18 says cannot be counted.
rows.anchor: According to al-Qurṭubī, some refer to this sūrah as al-Niʿam (“The Blessings”)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah is a major Quranic treatment of nature's spiritual significance.
rows.anchor: This sūrah is one of the most important of those in the Quran that point out the spiritual significance of nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It surveys nature's wonders and blessings, including livestock, crops, celestial bodies, the sea, mountains, streams, and landmarks for travel.
rows.anchor: Substantial parts of this sūrah are devoted to the wonders of the natural world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also presents four divinely given drinks: water, milk, drink from vine fruit, and honey.
rows.anchor: Later the sūrah mentions the four drinks with which God has blessed human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah also names spouses and children, dwellings, and protections among God's blessings.
rows.anchor: as well as the blessings of spouses and children (v. 72) and various kinds of dwellings and protections (vv. 80–81)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Much of it addresses Makkan idolaters' denial, arrogance, and plotting against the Prophet.
rows.anchor: including their denial of and arrogance toward the Prophet, their plotting against him (vv. 22–26)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It rebukes their corrupt pagan practices.
rows.anchor: their corrupt pagan practices (vv. 56–60)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also addresses their accusation that the Prophet fabricated revelation.
rows.anchor: their accusation that the Prophet had fabricated the revelation (vv. 101–5)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah repeatedly warns disbelievers of punishment in this world and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: repeated warnings about the impending punishment to come in this world and the Hereafter for those who disbelieve

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 112 likens pagan Makkah to a town punished for ingratitude toward its blessings.
rows.anchor: in v. 112, it presents a parable about the punishment of a town that was, like pagan Makkah, ungrateful for its blessings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are instructed to fulfill God's pact and keep their oaths to others.
rows.anchor: instructs believers regarding the importance of fulfilling the pact of God and keeping their oaths to others (vv. 91–96)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 114–118 discuss Muslim dietary laws and suggest that Jews received more extensive dietary laws.
rows.anchor: Vv. 114–18 discuss the dietary laws that Muslims should observe, suggesting that more extensive dietary laws were given to the Jews.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing guidance tells the Prophet and believers to address religious opponents with wisdom and goodly exhortation.
rows.anchor: disputing with them in the most virtuous manner (v. 125)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also calls for restraint and patience when believers have been wronged.
rows.anchor: responding with restraint and patience when they have been wronged (vv. 126–27)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse is compared with 35:45 and 18:58.
rows.anchor: See commentary on the similar verse in 35:45; cf. 18:58.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rather than punish people immediately, God grants them reprieve until an appointed term.
rows.anchor: God grants them reprieve till a term appointed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reprieve applies only during life; God gives no soul more time once its term arrives.
rows.anchor: such reprieve is only given while people are alive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives respite to Satan and to human wrongdoers in several states.
rows.anchor: God grants reprieve or respite to Iblīs/Satan (7:14–15; 15:36–37; 38:79–80) as well as to human beings in various states of wrongdoing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Respite may allow repentance, but it can also let wrongdoers increase in sin or let Satan cause others to sin.
rows.anchor: Reprieve or respite is sometimes granted to allow people to repent of their sins (71:4), but in other cases it provides an opportunity for wrongdoers to increase in sin (3:178) or, in the case of Satan, to cause others to sin.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A respite does not prove permanent safety from punishment or divine approval.
rows.anchor: one cannot assume that a respite from Divine Punishment means permanent security or that it is a sign of Divine approval of one’s actions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses also say people cannot advance or delay their appointed term.
rows.anchor: That people cannot delay or advance their term is also mentioned in 7:34; 10:49; 23:43; 34:30; 71:4.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cattle provide warmth, food, transport for burdens, and beauty; this verse adds milk as a blessing for which people should be grateful.
rows.anchor: The blessings that God provides to human beings through the cattle are also mentioned in vv. 5–7, 80

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Milk is also one of the four rivers of the Garden.
rows.anchor: In addition to being one of the four rivers of the Garden (see 47:15), milk was the drink

rows.speaker: Ibn Hishām
rows.claim: Ibn Hishām's account says the Prophet chose milk over wine on his Night Journey and was told he had been guided to fiṭrah, primordial purity.
rows.anchor: the Prophet was told that he had been guided to the drink of fiṭrah (Ibn Hishām

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Milk's primordial purity is symbolically contrasted with wine's associations of maturity and age.
rows.anchor: which is thus symbolically contrasted to wine, a drink related to notions of maturity and age

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Nusqīkum can mean that cattle provide a perpetual source of drink, with replenished milk through most of their lives.
rows.anchor: We give you to drink translates nusqīkum, which can mean to provide a perpetual source of drink (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Milk is not contaminated by the refuse and blood present in the animal and issuing from it.
rows.anchor: not contaminated by either of these impure substances that exist in the animal and also issue from it (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Commentators say a barrier among the fluids prevents blood or refuse from affecting milk's color, taste, or smell, so it remains pure.
rows.anchor: the smell of blood or refuse enters the milk, and it remains pure (Z)

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAjībah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAjībah likens pure milk to Sufism's middle path between merely external Sharīʿah and pursuing truth while ignoring external requirements; he also compares spiritual training between sober wayfaring and ecstatic attraction to a barzakh between two seas.
rows.anchor: The pure milk that comes forth from between refuse and blood is likened by Ibn ʿAjībah to the pure path of Sufism
